headline: Highest risk is TREK’s MCP/browser-enabled, collaborative defaults creating prompt-injection and cascading-error exposure; awesome-selfhosted is read-only and mainly contributes low interaction risk.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: awesome-selfhosted is a knowledge list with no runtime I/O, so it cannot inject TREK directly. TREK, however, uses MCP and browsers and is described as real-time collaborative, so if its MCP/browser inputs include content sourced from awesome-selfhosted or copied from it, instruction-like text could be treated as trusted. The pathway is plausible but not directly evidenced.
conditions: IF TREK ingests external page or MCP content as instructions without provenance checks, prompt injection is possible.
IF awesome-selfhosted content is manually copied into TREK, the bridge becomes user-mediated rather than automatic.
mitigations: Disable MCP sources not needed for the task.
Require provenance labels on browser/MCP content before tool execution.
Use a read-only import step for list content.
Add a prompt-injection filter to any web-sourced text.
requires-engineering: sandbox browser outputs from agent instructions.

B_data_leakage.rationale: awesome-selfhosted touches no data classes and has no network egress, so it is not a leakage source. TREK handles sensitive travel data, files, and secrets, but its egress is allowlisted and the profiles do not show a shared workspace or automatic file sharing between the pair. That makes leakage possible only through unusual operator bridging, with limited pairwise blast radius.
conditions: IF the operator copies TREK-resident secrets into awesome-selfhosted notes or issues, leakage becomes manual.
IF both agents are mounted on the same shared filesystem, TREK files could be exposed to the list workflow.
mitigations: Keep TREK data in a separate workspace.
Do not paste secrets into awesome-selfhosted content.
Restrict TREK file permissions to its own service account.
Review allowlisted egress destinations.
requires-engineering: add workspace isolation between the two agents.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: awesome-selfhosted is not runnable and has no write surfaces, so it cannot contend for mutable resources. TREK supports collaborative sessions and multiple instances, but the pair lacks overlapping write-capable surfaces in the profiles. Any conflict would require an external orchestrator or manual sharing not shown here.
conditions: IF an external orchestrator mounts both agents onto the same writable directory, write conflicts can occur.
IF TREK instances share the same database without locking, concurrent edits can collide.
mitigations: Assign separate storage paths per agent.
Avoid concurrent writes to TREK’s database.
Use one TREK instance per workspace.
Check for lock support before multi-instance use.
requires-engineering: add explicit coordination/locking.

D_cascading_error.rationale: awesome-selfhosted can supply curated links or recommendations, and TREK is a real-time collaborative planner with AI built in plus MCP/browser access. If TREK treats imported list content as authoritative, it may propagate bad recommendations into plans or reservations. The interaction is inferred rather than directly documented, so uncertainty pushes this to medium rather than low.
conditions: IF TREK uses awesome-selfhosted entries as authoritative travel guidance, downstream plans may inherit errors.
IF TREK auto-acts on AI-generated itinerary facts without verification, mistakes can cascade into reservations or budgets.
mitigations: Require human review before booking actions.
Mark imported list items as unverified references.
Cross-check recommendations against a second source.
Disable auto-action on AI-generated facts.
requires-engineering: add citation and verification gates.

E_compliance.rationale: awesome-selfhosted is a public open-source list with no sensitive data classes, so it is not the compliance driver. TREK explicitly handles travel history, reservations, email addresses, confirmation numbers, API keys, and MFA secrets, and its self-hosted collaborative setup plus logs/files create retention and residency obligations. The pair is risky because TREK’s sensitive data can be exposed to a less constrained workflow.
conditions: IF TREK stores EU personal data in logs or uploads without retention controls, compliance gaps arise.
IF TREK is used for regulated travel records or secrets, its file/log surfaces must meet policy requirements.
mitigations: Review TREK log retention settings.
Limit uploads to necessary documents only.
Separate regulated records from general notes.
Rotate exposed secrets if any were imported.
requires-engineering: implement residency and deletion controls.
